name: Uma Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Uma, 27, and I lead a contractor's electrical fault team, mostly homes and small business buildings. I have a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence; I earn above the usual rate and have ten months of living costs saved. I live alone, without children, and there are plenty of electrical employers nearby, so I can afford to be choosy. I use AI every day to organise my own fault notes, keeping customer details out, but the satisfying bit is still finding a loose connection behind a wall; what wears me out is being asked to make a junior faster before the junior is confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A useful note-writing tool doesn't need a revolution attached. We can use the few saved minutes to explain a fault properly to the junior. I'd rather finish a day with someone understanding the circuit than claim another imaginary efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and money feel secure here. I've a well-paid job, ten months of costs saved, and several local employers I could approach without packing up my home. If AI stays modest, I don't need to manufacture a crisis to justify being interested in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the fault team now and through the next year. Starting next month I'd ask the manager to keep a fifteen-minute paid fault discussion at the end of Friday's shift, using the time my note tool already saves. I'd continue the daily notes, checked against my actual readings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of relief that nobody needs to be frightened into trying a small improvement. I can enjoy the tools and still enjoy turning the phone off after work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you discuss in that Friday session?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the job where an intermittent light fault made us suspect the wrong cable. The junior could explain what measurement changed our minds, rather than listen to me give a little speech. That's fifteen minutes that could save a wrong diagnosis later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you simply add that session to the rota yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager first because I don't control everyone's paid time. If the discussion wasn't approved, I wouldn't make the junior stay unpaid. I'd keep explaining things within our existing site work instead.

say: I'd call the **note tool** useful without attaching a revolution to it.
I'd use saved minutes to help a **junior understand** a fault rather than boast about speed.
think: My **well-paid work** and ten-month reserve make this a secure picture for me.
Several **nearby employers** give me choices without requiring a house move.
do: Continue leading the **fault team** and checking daily AI notes against measurements.
Request a **paid Friday discussion** next month, keeping teaching within existing shifts if refused.
feel: **Calm and relieved**, able to enjoy useful tools without turning every improvement into a crisis.
S0.quote: A useful note-writing tool doesn't need a revolution attached.
fieldNote: Her **ten-month reserve** and plentiful local work support genuine security in the modest-change scenario.
A paid team discussion needs **manager approval**; individual teaching is not presented as collective organising or unpaid overtime.

steps.text: Keep leading electrical faults and checking daily AI-assisted notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the booking and checking work changes before the hands pulling cable. We should decide together what happens to the saved time. I'd ask our workers' association to put paid learning and a share of productivity gains on the agenda, rather than let every saving become a faster target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own fault-finding hours and income to remain secure in the next few years. The changes around the office make me uneasy, because a colleague's secure week shouldn't depend on whether a task looks physical. I have room to speak up without fearing that one awkward meeting will cost my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd bring a proposal to the workers' association for paid learning time for office and site staff. During the first year I'd learn the new AI fault-note checking features in a free practice account, then compare suggestions with twenty real jobs before recommending anything. I'd keep the work data anonymous and the actual electrical tests unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the team, but not frightened about my own bank account. I find the tool interesting. The hard part of using AI at work is asking who gets a better week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you include the office staff in that proposal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the booking staff to describe which calls don't fit the tidy categories before writing the proposal. I don't want a senior electrician turning up with a plan that erases someone else's work. The association meeting needs their words, not just mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle customer information during the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd remove names, addresses and photographs before entering any practice notes. If a problem needed identifiable site detail, I'd keep that example out of the account. Learning the tool doesn't give me permission to share a customer's home.

say: I'd say **office tasks change first**, while cable work still needs hands on site.
I'd ask the association to seek **paid learning** and a shared gain from saved time.
think: My own **hours and income** look secure over the next few years because fault-finding remains physical.
I'm uneasy about **colleagues' weeks** and can afford to question how the gains are distributed.
do: Bring a **paid-learning proposal** to the workers' association now with office staff's input.
Learn the **AI checking features** and compare anonymous notes with twenty completed jobs.
feel: **Uneasy for colleagues**, while interested in the tool and secure about her own finances.
S1.quote: The hard part of using AI at work is asking who gets a better week.
fieldNote: She explicitly distinguishes **personal security** from concern for colleagues, supporting an uneasy rather than anxious mood.
Association work involves **shared terms**, while the technical trial uses anonymous notes and retains actual electrical testing.

steps.text: Propose paid learning for office and site staff through the association
Learn AI note-checking features using anonymous records from twenty jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association we need agreements before 2028, not a promise to talk after people's hours fall. The thinking systems arrive then, and the hands-on robots around 2031. I'd want those different dates on the page so office workers aren't asked to wait for the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could shrink by the time capable robots spread, and a crowded local market could make today's plentiful alternatives less useful. Ten months saved gives me options, but it isn't a lifetime income. I think I can steer through some of this, though not by assuming my licence makes me immune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd enrol in a twelve-week evening course on maintaining building control systems, paying its fee from a separate study budget without touching the ten-month reserve. In 2029 I'd apply for posted maintenance roles that include on-site fault work, only accepting written pay and hours that cover my bills. I'd also work through the association on paid transition terms for both office and site staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with energy to act rather than a feeling of being trapped. I can afford the course and still eat if a job application fails. That margin is a privilege, not evidence that everybody can do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why choose that course if machines could affect maintenance too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course is one practical experiment, not a claim that building controls escape AGI. I'd ask working technicians what still needs on-site testing and check real vacancies before changing jobs. I could be wrong about demand and stop spending after that course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the agreement actually need to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the association for a written proposal on notice, paid learning and income support during agreed training. Those terms aren't in place just because I want them. I'd keep taking my electrical wage while we argued for a workable agreement.

say: I'd seek **agreements before 2028**, rather than wait until hours have already fallen.
I'd distinguish **office workers' timing** from the capable robot work arriving around 2031.
think: My own **hours could shrink**, and plentiful employers might offer fewer alternatives when machines spread.
The **ten-month reserve** gives options, without guaranteeing income for the rest of my working life.
do: Enrol now in the **twelve-week evening course**, using the separate study budget and preserving emergency savings.
Apply in **2029** for posted maintenance roles with on-site work and bill-covering written terms.
Work through the **association** on notice, paid learning and transition income support.
feel: **Anxious and active**, aware that her financial margin makes experiments possible without guaranteeing success.
S2.quote: Ten months saved gives me options, but it isn't a lifetime income.
fieldNote: She treats **controls study** as a funded experiment and explicitly rejects claims that maintenance is a permanently protected field.
The **2029 job search** is conditional on real vacancies and written terms, while proposed association protections remain unconfirmed.

steps.text: Enrol in the twelve-week controls course using the separate study budget
Seek posted maintenance work in 2029 with bill-covering written pay and hours
Negotiate notice and paid transition terms through the workers’ association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us test the training before calling it a solution. We should still negotiate now, including office staff who face the thinking systems in 2031. Robot work around 2034 gives the site team more time, not permission to forget everybody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My present pay and reserve look secure for the next few years, and I can test another role well before the later robot work. I'm uneasy about making the wrong bet, but I don't expect a near-term personal income loss in this picture. A five-year warning gives my experiments time to fail cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the twelve-week controls course now from the separate study budget and keep my current fault-team wage. Before 2031 I'd review vacancies each year instead of buying the next qualification automatically. In 2032 I'd apply only for actual maintenance roles with enough on-site work and written pay covering bills, while continuing the association's paid-transition proposal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a thoughtful rather than a breathless way. I can try the course, discover I dislike that work, and still have time to change my mind. I'd like the same room for people without my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether the course had been worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether I'd actually enjoyed tracing a building-control fault, not just whether the tutor passed me. Then I'd compare that with advertised duties and wages. A certificate that earns applause but doesn't lead to work isn't a reason to buy another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why seek covered fees if you can pay for your course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association that my ability to pay isn't a model for everyone. Our proposal should ask for paid time and covered fees, not tell staff to raid household accounts. I'd still pay for my own early experiment because I can afford it.

say: I'd say **five years** allows testing a course before claiming it solves the transition.
I'd include **office staff** in early negotiations instead of treating the site team's extra time as everyone's.
think: My **near-term pay** and reserve look secure while I test another role before later robot work.
I'm uneasy about a **wrong training bet**, but I have time to discover mistakes without a financial crisis.
do: Take the **twelve-week course** now from the separate study budget, retaining current paid work.
Review vacancies annually and apply in **2032** only for suitable jobs with bill-covering written terms.
Continue the **association proposal** for paid time and covered transition fees.
feel: **Uneasy with room** to test, and concerned that colleagues should receive similar room through agreed support.
S3.quote: A five-year warning gives my experiments time to fail cheaply.
fieldNote: Her milder mood follows an explicit expectation of **secure near-term income**, supported by savings and an early funded experiment.
She distinguishes **personal affordability** from the association's proposed terms, without treating unagreed funding as an existing entitlement.

steps.text: Take the controls course from the separate study budget while retaining wages
Seek suitable maintenance vacancies in 2032 on bill-covering written terms
Pursue paid learning time and covered fees through the association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance to make learning part of a normal paid week. I don't want a decade of warning used to make every worker responsible for solving this alone. I'd still turn up to the association meeting even when my own diary was full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel secure about my own work and living over the next few years, and the chance to test new work looks positive. At 37 in 2036 I'd still need earnings after thinking AGI and then robots around 2039, so I'd keep reviewing rather than declare myself finished. My current cushion lets me make changes from choice instead of a rent deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the short controls course now and ask the association to keep pressing for paid learning in normal shifts. Each year I'd compare actual duties, wages and my savings before paying for more study. During 2037 I'd apply for a suitable posted maintenance role only with bill-covering written terms; if my present work stayed better, I'd keep doing it and review again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own position, and interested in what I could build over that time. That's not a prediction that everyone will land safely. It's a description of having money and useful work while I try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you protect outside work during that long preparation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep making music with my friends on Wednesday nights instead of turning every evening into a course. If preparation swallows the life it's supposed to protect, I'd change the timetable. The long warning should make room for a life, not just a longer homework list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might make you act earlier than planned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch actual booked hours, what equipment the firm buys and what maintenance jobs offer. If those changed sooner, I'd advance the search rather than worship the date 2036. A yearly review is a decision point, not a promise to stay still between reviews.

say: I'd seek **paid learning** inside a normal week rather than leave everyone to solve the transition alone.
I'd keep attending **association meetings** even while my own paid work remains plentiful.
think: My own **near-term position** feels secure, and funded experiments look like an opportunity rather than an urgent escape.
At **37 in 2036**, I'll still need future earnings, so I'd keep checking actual work and savings.
do: Take the **short controls course** now and review real work before paying for further study.
Pursue **paid learning** through the association during ordinary preparation years.
Seek suitable vacancies in **2037** only on bill-covering written terms, retaining better current work if appropriate.
feel: **Calm and curious** about her own options, without claiming that everybody has the same financial room.
S4.quote: The long warning should make room for a life, not just a longer homework list.
fieldNote: Calm reflects **personal security** and affordable experiments, while future earnings remain a live issue rather than assumed retirement.
Her **2037 search** retains conditions and can advance if actual hours or equipment orders change sooner.

steps.text: Take the short controls course from the separate study budget
Pursue paid learning in normal shifts through the workers’ association
Seek suitable maintenance roles in 2037 only on bill-covering written terms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my own hours could fall once robots follow before I've tested another route. A written transition agreement with notice, paid study time and income support would help, especially for colleagues without my reserve. My savings can buy a course, but my colleagues need paid Tuesdays too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether learning is fun when it isn't tied to a threat. I actually like working out a new fault and showing someone else what I found. I'd like a future with more of that curiosity and less fear about who gets the next shift.

headlineQuote: My savings can buy a course, but my colleagues need paid Tuesdays too.
portrait: At **27**, Uma leads electrical faults with a technical diploma and master licence, higher pay, and ten months of expenses saved.
She lives **alone**, has no children, uses AI daily, and has plentiful nearby electrical employers to consider.
Her **progressive outlook** turns personal room to experiment into association proposals for paid learning and transition support.
Only the fastest picture makes her **anxious** about her own hours; longer warnings permit affordable tests without assuming another trade stays safe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her later hours before she has tested a different paid route.
whatWouldHelp: A **written transition agreement** covering notice, paid study time and income support would help, especially for colleagues without her reserve.
